‎مستحق الحرف is what the letter is owed because of where it happens to sit. The noon of مِن is an ordinary noon said in isolation; put ب after it and it becomes a mim hidden behind a hum. The alif of مَا is two counts alone; put a hamzah after it at the head of the next word and Hafs holds it four or five. Nothing about the letter itself changed, only its neighbourhood. Every rule from the Nun Sakin chapter onward lives in this second category; the two chapters before it, Articulation Points and Letter Qualities, are the haqq half of the same pair. That is exactly why none of the neighbour rules appear in an alphabet chart and all of them appear the moment letters stand next to each other.

Set against Hafs, the different-word bucket runs from 136 words (Shu'bah, who studied under the same teacher) to 1,561 (Ibn Wardan). Even the largest is two percent of the text, and every one of those words was transmitted, not chosen.

There is a classical way to find a letter's makhraj yourself, and it takes about five seconds. Put the letter in sukoon, prefix a hamza carrying a fatha, and say it slowly: أَقْ، أَبْ، أَسْ. Listen for the point where the sound is cut off. That point is the exit. For letters whose sound trails away instead of stopping cleanly, double the letter instead and feel where the friction sits: أَسّ، أَشّ. Ibn al-Jazari gives exactly this method, and it beats any diagram, because it is your own mouth reporting rather than someone else's description.

In the Quran, this Madd can fall under 3 main long-Madd cases from Tajweed: Madd Muttassil, Madd Munfasil, and Madd Lazim.
Madd Lazim (مَدّ لَازِم) means "necessary Madd." Lazim means necessary or required because the Madd letter is followed by a permanent sukoon or shaddah, so it is lengthened 6 counts.
Ending madd applies when you stop on a word and the ending sound changes because of waqf. It includes Madd Aarid lis-Sukoon and Madd Leen.
Length: 2, 4, or 6 counts. Madd Leen should follow the stopping style you choose for Madd Aarid lis-Sukoon, and should not be longer than it.
A special, “ruled” (hukmi) form of Madd Munfasil. The madd letter and the hamzah are written inside one word, so it looks like Madd Muttasil, but it is recited as a separated madd.
Length: 2, 4, or 5 counts (treated exactly like Madd Munfasil; be consistent)

Because the hamzah is in the following word, scholars classify this separately from muttasil. Allowed lengths vary by riwayah, so learners should follow one taught pattern and avoid switching counts randomly in the same recitation. This color also marks Madd Munfasil Hukmi ("ruled" separated). In a handful of words, the vocative يَٰٓ ("O…") and demonstrative هَٰٓ ("these…") particles are written joined to a following hamzah, such as يَٰٓأَيُّهَا and هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ; there, only that superscript-particle sequence is treated as separated even though it sits inside one written word.

Since both elements occur inside one word, this is treated as a stronger extension than natural madd. Keep the elongation measured and stable according to your riwayah so the hamzah after it remains clear and not swallowed. Note one exception: in the يَٰٓ/هَٰٓ particle words (e.g. يَٰٓأَيُّهَا, هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ) the superscript madd before the hamzah is recited as Madd Munfasil Hukmi instead, but any real madd letter + hamzah elsewhere in those same words (e.g. لَآءِ in هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ) stays muttasil.

‎الإشمام, in تَأۡمَ۬نَّا at Yusuf 12:11. The word underneath is تَأۡمَنُنَا, two noons that merged. Hafs is read with two accepted wajhs here. In the first you make the merge fully, and while saying the doubled noon you round your lips toward the damma that was dropped: a gesture with no sound in it, meant to be seen rather than heard. In the second, الاختلاس, you sound most of the dropped damma, about two thirds of it, on the first noon, so the merge is only partial and the ear catches a trace of it. This is not the الرَّوم of the previous lesson: الرَّوم is a way of stopping and sounds about a third of the vowel, while الاختلاس belongs to a joined reading. Both are read; a teacher will tell you which one is being taught. Note that this is a different thing from the ishmam that may be used at any stop, which the previous lessons mentioned.
